facts.title: A militia caught mid-action
facts.body: Rembrandt’s 1642 civic-guard portrait — wrongly nicknamed Night Watch — shows Captain Frans Banninck Cocq’s company stepping into motion under a stone arch. It is drama disguised as group portraiture.

facts.title: Captain Cocq in black
facts.body: Frans Banninck Cocq, center-left in black with a red sash, extends a hand that casts a shadow on his lieutenant — command made visible.

facts.title: Lieutenant in gold
facts.body: Willem van Ruytenburch’s pale gold costume catches Rembrandt’s spotlight. Hierarchy is written in cloth and light.

facts.title: The company mascot girl
facts.body: A brightly lit girl with a chicken at her belt may personify the Kloveniers (the bird was their emblem). She is allegory walking through a muster.

facts.title: The drummer at the edge
facts.body: At right a drummer starts the march. Sound enters a silent painting.

facts.title: Muskets in three stages
facts.body: Rembrandt shows loading, firing, and blowing powder — a mini-manual of arms woven into the crowd.

facts.title: The company’s colors
facts.body: The standard rises behind the officers, anchoring civic identity above the swirl of bodies.

facts.title: An arch like a stage
facts.body: The architectural arch frames the company as if they are exiting a gate into Amsterdam’s streets.

facts.title: A dog startled by the drum
facts.body: A small dog recoils near the drummer — comic noise in a solemn commission.

facts.title: Chiaroscuro as spotlight
facts.body: Rembrandt picks faces and fabrics out of brown shadow like a theatre lamp. “Night” was varnish and dirt; the drama was always daylight theatre.
